subject: phy
title: Electricity
subtitle: Charge, current, potential difference, resistance and Ohm's law.
concept: Electric current is the rate of flow of charge; conventional current flows from + to − (opposite to electron flow).
Potential difference is the energy transferred per unit charge; resistance is the ratio of p.d. to current.
Resistivity is a material property; resistance depends on resistivity, length and cross-sectional area: R = ρL/A.

notes.heading: Charge and Current
items: Current I = ΔQ/Δt; rate of flow of charge.
Electron drift velocity: I = nqvA (n = number density of charge carriers, q = charge on each, v = drift velocity, A = cross-sectional area).
Conventional current: + to −; electron flow: − to +.

notes.heading: Potential Difference and EMF
items: Potential difference (p.d.): energy transferred per unit charge between two points; V = W/Q; unit: volt (V = J C⁻¹).
EMF (ε): work done per unit charge by the source in moving charge around the complete circuit.
Terminal p.d. = EMF − voltage drop across internal resistance: V = ε − Ir.

notes.heading: Resistance and Ohm's Law
items: Ohm's law: V ∝ I at constant temperature → R is constant.
Ohmic conductor: straight line through origin on V–I graph (e.g. metal wire at constant T).
Non-ohmic: filament lamp (R increases with T); diode (one-way flow); thermistor (R decreases with T); LDR (R decreases with light intensity).
Resistivity: R = ρL/A (ρ = resistivity in Ω m; L = length; A = cross-sectional area). ρ is a material property.

definitions.body: The rate of flow of electric charge: I = ΔQ/Δt; unit: ampere (A).
The energy transferred per unit charge between two points: V = W/Q; unit: volt (V).
The ratio of potential difference to current: R = V/I; unit: ohm (Ω).
A material property determining how strongly it opposes current flow: ρ = RA/L; unit: Ω m.
For an ohmic conductor at constant temperature, current is proportional to potential difference: V = IR.

workedExamples.q: A copper wire of length 2.0 m, diameter 0.50 mm, has resistivity 1.7×10⁻⁸ Ω m. Calculate its resistance.
A cell of EMF 12 V and internal resistance 2 Ω is connected to a 10 Ω resistor. Find the terminal p.d.

mistakes: Confusing EMF (energy input per charge by source) with terminal p.d. (energy available to external circuit) — they differ by the internal resistance drop.
Using V = IR with the wrong V — use p.d. across the component, not EMF of the cell.
Forgetting that resistivity (Ω m) is a material property; resistance (Ω) depends on dimensions.
tips: I = nqvA: wire with larger area carries more current at same drift velocity; higher carrier density → faster drift at same I.
LDR and thermistor are both non-ohmic: R decreases when light/temperature increases.
Drift velocity is very slow (~mm s⁻¹) but electrical signal propagates at ~c.

flashcards.q: What is the relationship between charge, current and time?
State the formula for drift velocity.
flashcards.a: I = nqvA (n = carrier density, q = charge, v = drift velocity, A = cross-sectional area).
Electromotive force: the work done per unit charge by the source in driving charge around the whole circuit; measured in volts.
ρ = RA/L (Ω m); a material property that determines how strongly a material opposes current flow.

flashcards.q: How does resistance of a thermistor change with temperature?
flashcards.a: Decreases as temperature increases — thermistors are non-ohmic (negative temperature coefficient, NTC).
The potential difference across the terminals of the cell: V = ε − Ir (EMF minus the internal resistance drop).

questions.q: A current of 2 A flows for 5 minutes. How much charge passes?
What does the gradient of a V–I graph represent?
questions.exp: Gradient = ΔV/ΔI = resistance. (Conductance = 1/R = ΔI/ΔV = gradient of I–V graph.)

questions.q: A 6 Ω resistor is made from a material with ρ = 3×10⁻⁶ Ω m, length 0.1 m. What is its area?
The terminal p.d. of a battery is less than its EMF because:
opts: Charge is lost in the battery
Energy is dissipated in the internal resistance
questions.exp: Terminal p.d. = ε − Ir; the difference (Ir) is the voltage drop across the internal resistance.

questions.q: Which device has resistance that decreases as light intensity increases?
questions.exp: LDR (light-dependent resistor): more light → more electron-hole pairs → lower resistance.

recall: Define current, potential difference and resistance in terms of energy and charge.
State Ohm's law and describe what an ohmic conductor looks like on a V–I graph.
Explain the difference between EMF and terminal p.d.
Use R = ρL/A to calculate resistance or resistivity.
Describe the V–I characteristics of a filament lamp, diode and thermistor.
